content:
Surprised there is no topic about this already, but math inc published a formalization of the erdos 1196 proof that is making the news rounds since discovered by ChatGPT (informally) a few days ago. I am not an expert in higher quality lean code nor the mathematics involved but by cursory glance https://github.com/math-inc/Erdos1196/tree/main looks like extra effort was taken this time to make the formalization more readable and maintainable (4k loc in total, well split into files and lemmas it seems). Curious to hear how the experts see it.

Also if anyone else has alternative formalizations feel free to share here

There were others solved the same day BTW:
https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/258 (Solved by @Przemek Chojecki with GPT-5.4 Pro)
Rumors are there was a third but I couldn't find it.

Thanks for the mention, I've also formalized with Aristotle my solution, except for one sorry related to Tao-Teräväinen work.

Also the third Erdos problem that was solved that day was this one: https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1197 and it was also formalized with Aristotle.

Altogether it was 3 different Erdos problems, 3 different people, all solved with GPT-5.4 and (partly) formalized within 24 hours.

Also this 1196 is making rounds because there was really an interesting technique used, and this problem wasn't completely unknown (as is the case with many Erdos problems, that they simply lack experts' attention). There's a very interesting discussion going on in the thread about it: https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1196

Przemek Chojecki said:

Also this 1196 is making rounds because there was really an interesting technique used, and this problem wasn't completely unknown (as is the case with many Erdos problems, that they simply lack experts' attention). There's a very interesting discussion going on in the thread about it: https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1196

I keep hearing this, though it seems to need some deep level of specific insight to appreciate it fully.

The thing is, if the hype is true, I am very surprised that this thread took so long to make, and is so inactive.

I wouldn't over hype it, this is a nice result, probably the nicest so far when it comes to Erdos problems, but I'd still say it's pretty niche as of now. There's however some potential for building a more general theory around the solution and solve some other Erdos problems this way.

But current LLMs are not at the level to build this theory without human guidance/prompting. You can even see that in the discussion, Terence Tao together with others basically nicely repackaged argument given by GPT: simplifying it, and also finding the core of it (invariant measure).

To me, this is definitely the coolest Erdos AI solution so far - in part because I knew about this problem before the erdosproblems.com website, and earlier progress on it was already noteworthy: https://www.quantamagazine.org/graduate-students-side-project-proves-prime-number-conjecture-20220606/

@Paul Lezeau added this to Formal Conjectures:
https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/theorem/?name=Erdos1196.erdos_1196
and has a WIP pull request to formalise the solution:
FC#3760
I'd like to see Terry's proof that's two paragraphs (omitting some estimates) long formalised.
Isn't Paul's PR above - https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3760/changes based on Tao's proof (I don't understand the math well enough to answer that myself).

David Michael Roberts said:

I'd like to see Terry's proof that's two paragraphs (omitting some estimates) long formalised.

Is this the proof you have in mind @David Michael Roberts ?

David Michael Roberts said:

https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1196#post-5521

#34028 is an attempt at adding flows, although only on finite graphs, which might be a nice start towards that.
Maybe we can rework it to support infinite graphs which are locally-finite, and then perhaps a separate version that imports topology and can use tsum to define flows on infinite graphs which might not be locally-finite such as Tao's graph IIUC.
(Note that working with SimpleGraph rather than Digraph is fine, it's more general. The tsum version might even get away with only using completeGraph V.)
@Snir Broshi nice. That's the kind of general-purpose tooling we love to see developed as a result of cool new theorems.
